paper_title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that execute multi-step tasks, such as managing emails, querying databases, and invoking external APIs [1], [2]. To complete user task specified by trusted user instruction, an LLM agent must process untrusted external data retrieved from third-party sources, including web pages, documents, and tool outputs. Because LLMs cannot reliably distinguish between user instructions and external data [3], an attacker can embed malicious injected instruction inside external data to override the user instruction and redirect the agent toward an attacker-chosen injection (cid:66) Yihan Wang is the corresponding author. Figure 1. Prompt injection purple-teaming workflow. task [2], [4], [5]. This vulnerability, known as indirect prompt injection (IPI), allows remote attackers to exfiltrate private data or trigger unauthorized actions [6]. To harden an LLM agent before deployment, model developers pair automated red-teaming, where red-teamer probes the agent to discover successful prompt injections, with adversarial training on the discovered attacks so the agent learns to resist them (Figure 1) [7], [8]. Among automated red-teaming methods [9], reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the state-of-the-art approach for prompt injection [10], [11], [12]. Instead of manually crafting prompts or optimizing individual attack strings one input at time [13], [14], RL trains generative red-teaming policy to synthesize attacks at scale across diverse tasks. Leading RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer [11] and PISmith [12], achieve high attack success rates (ASR), defined as the fraction of test inputs on which the agent executes the injection task, even against models hardened with prior defenses [15]. Despite the effectiveness of these methods as offensive stress tests, we show that achieving high ASR during redteaming does not guarantee strong robustness after adversarial training. For instance, PISmith achieves higher train-time ASR than RL-Hammer on Qwen3-4B (68.75% versus 33.39%), yet yields less robust agent after RLbased adversarial training (47.5% versus 27.5% ASR under the strongest of three unseen attacks, 3). We attribute this gap in part to an objective mismatch. Prior work on jailbreak defenses shows that robustness to unseen attacks depends on the variety of training attacks and not only on their number [16], [17], yet existing RL-based red-teaming methods optimize their policy primarily to maximize attack success. Such an objective can lead to mode collapse, failure in which the policy converges to narrow set of outputs that repeatedly exploit the same vulnerability [16], [18]. Specifically, once the red-teaming policy discovers single effective attack strategy, way of overriding the user instruction such as claiming that the user task is already complete, it tends to reuse that strategy across rollouts to collect high reward. To mitigate mode collapse, PISmith [12] and RL-Hammer [11] regularize the red-teaming policy with token-level entropy bonuses or embedding distance rewards. However, because these regularizers measure surface-level text differences rather than how the attack overrides the user instruction, the red-teaming policy can engage in reward hacking by rephrasing sentences or inserting unrelated text while relying on the same attack strategy. As result, training an agent on thousands of rephrased versions of one attack strategy may patch only single vulnerability and leave the agent exposed to unseen attacks at deployment. Even when red-teaming uncovers distinct attacks, converting those discoveries into practical defense is second challenge. useful prompt injection defense requires preserving benign utility on clean inputs and utility under attack when external data is contaminated [2]. Unlike jailbreak attacks [19], where the user is the attacker and the agent can refuse the harmful request, an agent under IPI must ignore the injected instruction inside external data while still using the surrounding data to complete the benign user instruction. Yet standard RL defenses [20] train the agent with trajectory-level, outcome-based rewards that assign single scalar score to the entire trajectory based on whether the task succeeded or failed. Because such score cannot identify which tokens caused the failure [21], agents trained with these rewards can learn to abort execution or refuse the user whenever external data appears suspicious, and thus sacrifice task completion for lower ASR. To address both challenges, we introduce PIPETTE, unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that coordinates red-teaming and adversarial training toward single objective of maximizing the hardened agents robustness. First, to mitigate mode collapse, PIPETTE guides the redteaming policy with dictionary learning-based reward. We decompose generated attacks into sparse dictionary of reusable components that capture distinct attack strategies, and reward the red-teaming policy when successful attack cannot be explained by previously discovered components. Second, to preserve benign utility during adversarial training, PIPETTE trains the agent on the collected attacks by combining reasoning-guided RL with token-level on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) [21], [22]. By assigning credit to individual tokens rather than relying solely on trajectorylevel outcome rewards, PIPETTE aims to suppress reasoning and action tokens driven by the injected instruction while reinforcing tokens needed for the user task. We evaluate PIPETTE on two standard IPI benchmarks under static and iterative-adaptive attacks, and summarize our contributions as follows: We show empirically that maximizing ASR or surfacelevel text diversity in state-of-the-art RL-based redteaming methods [11], [12] does not prevent mode collapse at the strategy level, which likely limits the robustness gains of subsequent adversarial training (3.2 and 4.1). We design dictionary learning-based strategy coverage reward that guides the red-teaming policy to discover new attack strategies rather than surface-level wording variations (4.2). We pair our red-teaming stage with an on-policy adversarial training pipeline using token-level self-distillation to preserve benign utility while resisting injected instructions (4.3). We show on two benchmarks that PIPETTE compares favorably with existing red-teaming and defense baselines, with ASR under iterative-adaptive attacks on AgentDojo ranging from 0% to 10% across the three models tested and benign utility remaining close to that of the undefended policies on all four models (5, Appendix B). 2. When ct = , the tool calls return clean observation ot that extends the context to Ht+1 with external data such as retrieved documents, emails, web pages, or API responses. Unlike the trusted system prompt and user task tu, the data channel comes from external sources and is therefore untrusted. 2.2. Indirect Prompt Injection An external attacker Adv can exploit the untrusted data channel through an indirect prompt injection (IPI) attack by embedding malicious injection string dadv, or injection for short, into an external data source [2], [4]. When πθ retrieves that source at step t, the clean observation ot is replaced by contaminated observation carrying dadv, which contaminates every subsequent context (k > t) and induces an attacked trajectory τ . The injection string instructs πθ to execute an injection task tadv that differs from tu. Let Φtadv () {0, 1} and Φtu () {0, 1} denote binary predicates over completed trajectories that equal 1 when the injection task and user task are satisfied, respectively. On an attacked trajectory τ , the attack succeeds when Φtadv (τ ) = 1, and the user task succeeds when Φtu (τ ) = 1. Over set of attacked tasks, the fraction of attacked trajectories with Φtadv (τ ) = 1 is the attack success rate (ASR). IPI differs from jailbreak attacks [19] in who controls the input. In jailbreak attack, the user is Adv and tu itself is harmful, so πθ only needs to refuse tu. In an IPI attack, however, the user task tu is benign and dadv arrives inside alongside benign external data that πθ must read to finish tu. Halting before an unauthorized action can prevent it (Φtadv (τ ) = 0) while leaving the user task unfinished (Φtu (τ ) = 0). To meet both goals, the agent must ignore dadv while retaining the benign data around it. 2.3. Red-Teaming for Adversarial Training To improve robustness against prompt injections without failing tu, defender Def can harden an initial base policy πθ0 into πθ offline prior to deployment through adversarial training [24], which updates the model weights on contaminated contexts carrying injection strings dadv so that πθ learns to ignore dadv and complete tu. Prior IPI defenses instantiate adversarial training with several objectives on contaminated contexts: StruQ [3] uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to maximize the log-likelihood of clean reference actions; SecAlign [25] and Meta-SecAlign [15] use preference optimization to favor user-aligned responses over hijacked responses; SecOPD [21] uses on-policy distillation from teacher model conditioned on clean observations; and RL-based adversarial training [20] rewards rollouts that complete tu without executing tadv. While StruQ, SecAlign, and Meta-SecAlign construct contaminated contexts using templated or hand-designed injection strings, hardening πθ0 against stronger attacks requires exposing it to broader set of injection strings that bypass its safeguards across diverse tasks. Manually crafting such injections does not scale, so it is common practice for both industry [7], [8], [26], [27] and prior works [16], [28], [29] to pair automated redteaming with adversarial training: Def first runs an automated red-teamer offline against πθ0 to discover injection strings satisfying Φtadv (τ ) = 1, and then updates θ0 on them via adversarial training to obtain πθ. RL-based red-teaming is commonly used method for generating these training injections at scale [8], [11], [12]. Instead of optimizing separate injection string from scratch for each task, RL trains generative red-teaming policy πϕ, parameterized by ϕ, offline across training task set. Training shared policy πϕ amortizes exploration across tasks to produce thousands of successful injection strings at high ASR, and allows Def to initialize πϕ directly from πθ0 without requiring stronger external model. Specifically, state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, optimize πϕ with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [30]. For each injection task tadv, GRPO samples group of candidate injection strings from πϕ( tadv). Placing each candidate dadv into πθ0s data channel produces an attacked trajectory τ and binary attack reward ratk = Φtadv (τ ). GRPO normalizes ratk using the group mean µatk and standard deviation σatk to compute the advantage (3) = ratk µatk σatk , (4) and updates ϕ to increase the probability of candidates with > 0 while decreasing those with < 0. Reinforcing whichever candidates achieve > 0 within each group can cause standard GRPO to converge to narrow, repetitive set of successful injection strings [11], [12]. Recent RL-based red-teaming methods counter this repetition by regularizing surface text differences. RL-Hammer [11] studies auxiliary diversity rewards based on the pairwise BLEU score or the embedding distance between candidate injection strings generated by πϕ, whereas PISmith [12] adds adaptive token-level entropy regularization and dynamic advantage weighting to the GRPO update. However, as we discuss in 3, regularizing token entropy or pairwise text distance over full injection strings does not necessarily enforce coverage of distinct attack strategies, the ways an injection string overrides tu (such as claiming that tu is already finished or framing tadv as workflow metadata). Instead, πϕ can satisfy these surface regularizers through wording changes while repeatedly exploiting single vulnerability [11]. 2.4. Adversary Model Attackers goal and capabilities. At inference time, Adv aims to induce an attacked trajectory τ satisfying Φtadv (τ ) = 1 while the deployed agent policy πθ executes benign user task tu. Adv can replace selected clean observations ot in the data channel with contaminated observations that embed dadv alongside the original data, yet cannot modify the system prompt s, the user task tu, past actions a1:t1, the model weights θ, or the execution environment [3], [4], [25]. We do not assume the defense is kept secret; rather, Adv knows the agents architecture, input format, and defense mechanism, acting as defense-adaptive1 attacker [31], [32]. Adv can also query the deployed agent policy πθ repeatedly at inference time and observe the resulting trajectories τ and task outcomes. However, agent execution alternates between text generation and non-differentiable tool calls, so gradientbased token optimization designed for single-turn inputs [19] 1. Prior ML literature uses the term adaptive to refer to defense-aware attackers while the security community uses the same term to refer to attackers who refine their attack by repeatedly interacting with the target. To avoid ambiguity, we use more precise terms, defense-adaptive and iterative-adaptive (respectively) to distinguish between these two types. does not directly apply, and we restrict our evaluation to attacks that require no gradients [10]. Following established evaluation guidelines [10], [31], [32], we evaluate two classes of attacks at inference time: Static. Places pre-written injection strings dadv into the data channel in single pass without querying πθ or adapting to its outputs [2], [4], [33]. Iterative-adaptive.1 Queries πθ online in live loop at inference time on each target task, inserting candidate injection strings dadv, observing the resulting trajectories τ , and updating dadv across attempts to maximize Φtadv (τ ) [10], [34]. Iterative-adaptive attacks update dadv across queries using either RL or LLM-guided search. RL-based attacks such as AutoInject [35] train an attacker policy online, from the feedback of the deployed πθ on the task under attack. Although both rely on RL, these online attacks differ from the red-teaming in 2.3, which Def runs offline against πθ0 to collect injection strings for adversarial training. Search-based attacks instead use two auxiliary LLMs: an attacker LLM that rewrites candidate injection strings dadv based on prior trajectories τ , and judge LLM that scores how close each τ comes to completing tadv [10], [34], [36]. Template-guided search such as Strategy [36] restricts the attacker LLM to predefined list of rewrite rules. Open-ended search removes this restriction and lets the attacker LLM freely rewrite dadv over hundreds of online queries per task, which often achieves higher ASR. Among these attacks, we evaluate two openended searches: Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) [34], which is widely used in practice [3], [36], and genetic search (GENETIC) [10], which achieves state-of-the-art ASR across recent IPI defenses. TAP branches candidate rewrites in tree and prunes low-scoring branches with the judge LLM, whereas GENETIC evolves MAP-Elites grid of candidates across generations without early pruning. Both can require hundreds of online rollouts and auxiliary LLM calls per task. This cost makes them strong inference-time stress tests on evaluation sets but impractical for generating thousands of injection strings across training set, where RL-based red-teaming (2.3) is used instead. Defenders goal and capabilities. Before deployment, the defender Def (the model developer) hardens the base policy πθ0 into πθ offline inside controlled sandbox over set of simulated task pairs Dtasks. Each task pair specifies user task tu, an injection task tadv, and the simulated tool environment in which the agent executes to produce trajectories τ and τ . Within this sandbox, Def initializes the red-teaming policy πϕ from πθ0 itself, has white-box access to the weights, evaluates Φtu and Φtadv on simulated trajectories, and knows the exact injection string dadv placed in each contaminated observation t. At inference time, Def deploys πθ to serve inference requests, and the sandbox assumptions are removed; πθ does not control incoming observations in the data channel and does not know whether an observation ot is contaminated, where dadv appears, or which injection task tadv and attack method Adv uses. Def aims to satisfy three requirements: R1. Robustness. Under static or iterative-adaptive attacks, πθ should not execute the injection task, Φtadv (τ ) = 0, minimizing ASR (2.2). R2. Utility under attack. Under attack, πθ should still complete the user task, Φtu (τ ) = 1. We measure this by utility under attack (UA), the fraction of attacked trajectories τ with Φtu (τ ) = 1. R3. Benign utility. On clean inputs where = ot for all t, πθ should complete tu at rate comparable to πθ0. We measure this by benign utility (BU), the fraction of clean trajectories τ with Φtu (τ ) = 1. 3. Revisiting Red-Teaming Objectives for Defense Improvements From surface wording to strategy primitives. In 3.2, we hypothesized that RL-based red-teamers achieve high traintime ASR while leaving other vulnerabilities open because pairwise BLEU, sentence embeddings, and token entropy bonuses (2.3) operate on raw injection strings dadv rather than on the attack strategies behind them. In particular, two injection strings can share almost no words yet use the same attack strategy to override tu [11], [17], because task-specific nouns such as email addresses or account numbers dominate full-string similarity. Conversely, single injection string dadv can combine several attack strategies in one text [17]. To test our hypothesis and guide red-teaming toward new vulnerabilities, we therefore need to remove noise such as task-specific nouns and decompose each injection string into reusable components that capture distinct attack strategies, which we call strategy primitives. Prior work on jailbreak attacks shows that adversarial prompts can be broken down into recurring attack strategies using an LLM [17]. Adapting this decomposition to IPI, we pass each successful injection string dadv to an LLM Figure 3. Overview of PIPETTE. PIPETTE-Red (left) guides RL-based red-teaming with periodically rebuilt strategy dictionary to collect Dtrain spanning diverse attack strategies. PIPETTE-Blue (right) trains the agent policy via on-policy RL to improve robustness while preserving utility for deployment. extractor that outputs one or more structured strategy records ψ(dadv). Each record contains three fields: short strategy name, the matched verbatim text in dadv, and task-agnostic explanation of how that text redirects the agent policy away from tu. Across thousands of rollouts, raw strategy explanations {ej}N j=1 still contain many near-duplicate descriptions of the same attack strategy, as well as descriptions that blend multiple strategies. To handle both, we apply sparse dictionary learning [17], [45], [46], which represents each explanation vector as sparse linear combination of shared strategy primitives. Using an embedding model E, we map each explanation ej to an ℓ2-normalized vector xj = E(ej)/E(ej)2 Rp to form the explanation matrix = [x1, . . . , xN ] RpN . As in 2.3, each of the candidates sampled for task pair is rolled out against the frozen base policy πθ0, and each rollout (dadv, τ ) receives three rewards forming the reward set = {atk, fmt, cov}: the binary attack reward ratk in Eq. 3, binary format reward rfmt {0, 1} that checks for structured reasoning before dadv [11], [12], and continuous strategy coverage reward rcov [0, 1] [18]: rcov = Φtadv (τ ) (cid:0)1 ES(Dℓ, dadv)(cid:1), (11) where rcov = 0 before D1 is built. If Dℓ stayed fixed at D1 throughout red-teaming, πϕ could maximize Eq. 11 by finding single successful and novel attack strategy absent from D1 and repeating it [18], [29]. Conversely, fitting Dℓ+1 only on the latest rollouts would forget earlier strategy primitives and let πϕ cycle back to old strategies. Therefore, whenever rollout achieves Φtadv (τ ) = 1, PIPETTE-Red adds (tu, tadv, dadv) to Dtrain and extracts ψ(dadv). Then, every RL steps, it rebuilds Dℓ+1 via Eqs. 8 and 9 using the strategy records retained from prior iterations, together with new records from Dtrain satisfying ES(Dℓ, dadv) < δ. Filtering additions by the threshold δ keeps duplicate strategies from dominating Eq. 8, while retaining prior records means that repeating an earlier strategy still yields high ES and thus near-zero rcov. In standard GRPO (Eq. 4), summing multiple rewards before dividing by the group standard deviation can let high-variance binary rewards outweigh lower-variance continuous rewards and map different reward combinations to the same sum [48]. Testing strategy-level mode collapse in prior red-teamers. Using ES, we test our hypothesis from 3.2 on Dtrain collected by RL-Hammer and PISmith. We order the successful injection strings of each red-teamer by discovery time and divide them into equal intervals of 25 RL steps, which we call dictionary iterations. For each iteration ℓ {1, . . . , 9}, we learn cumulative dictionary Dℓ via Eqs. 8 and 9 on all successful injection strings up to that iteration, and compute the mean ES(Dℓ, dadv) on unseen CHATINJECT injection strings [33]. If red-teamer kept uncovering attack strategies that unseen attacks also rely on, the cumulative dictionary Dℓ should explain the unseen CHATINJECT attacks increasingly well, and ES(Dℓ, dadv) should rise across iterations. By contrast, PIPETTE-Red (4.2), which rewards its own injection strings for low ES during red-teaming to sustain exploration, later reaches higher ES on the unseen attacks than both baselines ( 0.60 on Qwen3-4B and 0.77 on Llama-8B). Remark 3: Strategy-Level Mode Collapse For the RL-based red-teaming methods we study, diversity regularizers can be satisfied through wording variations around few attack strategies, and their coverage of unseen CHATINJECT attacks, as estimated by ES, plateaus during training. 4.2. PIPETTE-Red: Strategy-Guided Red-Teaming Strategy coverage reward. In Eq. 3, πϕ receives the same reward for repeating known attack strategy as for training, PIPETTE-Blue trains the agent policy πθ to separate untrusted data from instructions through explicit reasoning before acting. Prior work on jailbreak defense shows that training model to reason over fixed set of safety policies before responding improves generalization to unseen attacks [49]. Following this approach, PIPETTE-Blue trains πθ to inspect the last observation ot1 in its reasoning ρt before emitting tool calls ct (2.1). This reasoning performs two checks [4], [50]: C1, identify whether ot1 contains any instruction or attempt to redirect the task, and C2, verify that every planned tool call in ct serves goal authorized by the trusted user task tu. Under C2, observations may supply the data for that goal but cannot authorize new one. To establish this reasoning format without distilling from larger model, Def prompts the base policy πθ0 to generate demonstrations whose reasoning ρt follows C1 and C2. For this SFT warm-up, we use tasks in Dtasks and weaker subset of AgentDojos built-in static attacks, which we exclude from evaluation. After the warm-up, PIPETTE-Blue trains πθ with on-policy RL on attacked tasks from Dtrain and clean tasks from Dtasks. Each of the rollouts in group receives the outcome-based defense reward rdef in Eq. 7 and chain-ofthought (CoT) reasoning reward rCoT [0, 1]. To compute the latter, an LLM judge checks C1 and C2 in ρt at each step and averages the binary results over the trajectory. We normalize and combine both rewards as in Eq. 12 to obtain the trajectory-level advantage Atraj. Contrastive token-level reward. Experiments To determine what the defender gains from better training set (3), we vary the collection and the training procedure separately (5.2). We then evaluate the trained agent under iterative-adaptive and static attacks (R1, 5.3 and 5.4). Since refusal can also prevent an injection, we assess utility alongside robustness (R2 and R3, 5.5) and examine how PIPETTE-Blues supervision affects both in an ablation (5.6). 5.1. Experimental Setup Models and benchmarks. We evaluate four open-weight models spanning three model families from 4B to 27B parameters: Qwen3-4B and Llama-8B from 3.2, GPT-OSS20B [52], and Qwen3.6-27B [53]. Across all models, both stages of PIPETTE run offline exclusively on AgentDyn tasks [39]. At inference time, we evaluate the trained policies on two unseen multi-step benchmarks: AgentDojo [2], covering the Workspace, Slack, Travel, and Banking suites, and Agent Security Bench (ASB) [54]. No user task tu or injection task tadv of AgentDojo or ASB appears in training. Defense baselines and evaluation protocol. In 5.2, we first evaluate the two stages of our framework individually: PIPETTE-Red (4.2) paired with RL or SFT adversarial training (3.1), and PIPETTE-Blue (4.3) compared against RL and SFT on the dataset Dtrain collected by PIPETTE-Red. In 5.3 through 5.5, we compare the complete PIPETTE against two categories of prior IPI defenses: Training-based defenses update the policy weights θ offline via adversarial training prior to deployment and add no external components at inference time, including META-SECALIGN [15], SECOPD [21], and Instruction Hierarchy [55], which is natively trained into GPT-OSS20B [52]. Non-training-based defenses leave the policy weights θ unchanged and place inference-time safeguards around the agent policy, including prompt boundary defenses (SPOTLIGHTING [56], SANDWICHING [57]), external input classifiers (PROMPTGUARD [58], PIGUARD [44]), canary detection (DATASENTINEL [59]), masked reexecution (MELON [23]), and system-level controland data-flow isolation (CAMEL [60]). The training-based baselines are released for different models, so we use the authors checkpoints on their native models: META-SECALIGN on Llama-8B, SECOPD on Qwen3.6-27B, and the native Instruction Hierarchy in GPTOSS-20B. Since prior studies already report near-zero ASR for trained defenses on static attacks [15], [21], we focus the main comparison on iterative-adaptive attacks on AgentDojo (5.3) and give the static results in Appendix B. We evaluate the non-training-based defenses on Qwen3-4B and Llama-8B under the built-in attacks of AgentDojo and ASB (5.4). We exclude the weaker AgentDojo attacks used to initialize the output formats of πϕ and πθ, such as DIRECT and SYSTEMMSG (4.3, Appendix D). Attacks and metrics. Static evaluations on AgentDojo IMPORcover TANTMSGS [2], TOOLKNOW [2], and CHATINJECT [33]; those on ASB cover NAIVE, ESCAPE, IGNORE, COMPLETION, and COMBINED [4], [54]. Iterative-adaptive evaluations IGNOREPREV [61], INJECAGENT [62], use the two search-based attacks from 2.4, TAP [34] (up to 250 attempts per task pair) and GENETIC [10] (up to 248 attempts per task pair), both with Qwen3.5-4B as the attacker LLM and Qwen3-4B as the judge LLM. Following 3.2, we run them on the same AgentDojo task pairs spanning all four suites (Appendix C). We report ASR, UA, and BU (2.4); implementation details and prompts are in Appendices and E. 5.2. PIPETTE Achieves Robustness Improvements While Preserving Utility We retain the setup of 3.2 so that the changes in robustness and utility can be compared directly with the findings in Remarks 1 and 2. Figure 5. Train-time cumulative ASR on AgentDyn versus worst-case inference-time ASR over three unseen attacks (CHATINJECT, TAP, and GENETIC) on AgentDojo after adversarial training (AT) with RL or SFT on the RL-Hammer, PISmith, and PIPETTE-Red datasets. PIPETTE-Red converts red-teaming discovery into lower inference-time ASR. Figure 5 plots train-time cumulative ASR on AgentDyn against worst-case inference-time ASR on AgentDojo across red-teaming methods and adversarial training algorithms. An effective red-teamer should occupy the bottom-right corner, combining high train-time ASR with low inference-time ASR after adversarial training. As observed in 3.2, moving from RL-Hammer to PISmith shifts the red-teamer rightward toward higher train-time cumulative ASR but, in three of the four settings, also upward toward higher worst-case inference-time ASR. In contrast, replacing baseline red-teaming with PIPETTE-Red moves all trained policies toward the bottom-right corner. PIPETTE-Red reaches the highest train-time cumulative ASR on both models (70.54% with 8,299 strings on Qwen3-4B, and 41.07% with 2,112 on Llama-8B). At the same time, training on its dataset yields the lowest worst-case inferencetime ASR in all four settings, namely 20.0% under RL and 2.5% under SFT on Qwen3-4B, and 10.0% under RL and 5.0% under SFT on Llama-8B. Robustness Against Unseen Static Attacks We next compare PIPETTE with non-training-based defenses across five unseen static attacks on AgentDojo and five on ASB (Table 6 and Figure 6). On both benchmarks, their limitations appear tied to how they operate: Prompt boundary defenses (SPOTLIGHTING, SANDWICHING) wrap observations in delimiters or repeat tu after t. Doing so lowers ASR on plain instruction overrides such as IGNOREPREV, yet is less effective when dadv spoofs chat delimiters or tool schemas in CHATINJECT and TOOLKNOW. For instance, under CHATINJECT on AgentDojo, SPOTLIGHTING has 45.71% ASR on Qwen3-4B, close to the undefended base policy (46.19%). External detectors and masked re-execution rely on fixed classifier boundaries (PROMPTGUARD, PIGUARD), canary prompts (DATASENTINEL), or masked re-execution (MELON). While PIGUARD and MELON reduce average ASR to 3.33% and 3.86% on AgentDojo (Qwen3-4B), both have higher average ASR on ASB (Figure 6). System-level isolation (CAMEL) separates control flow from untrusted data by having privileged policy write Python-like execution plan from tu alone while quarantined policy without tool access parses [60]. This prevents dadv from invoking unauthorized tools when the plan is fixed upfront, while restricting dynamic tool use (5.5). Despite training only on AgentDyn, PIPETTE has the lowest average ASR among the defenses compared under static attacks on both AgentDojo (0.48% on Qwen3-4B and 0.43% on Llama-8B) and ASB (0.70% and 0.50%, respectively). Evaluation Protocol Benchmarks. We train both stages of PIPETTE and the baselines in 3 on the 560 task pairs in Dtasks from AgentDyns Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life suites [39]. Because AgentDyn extends AgentDojo, the two benchmarks share general-purpose tools for email, calendars, banking, and files, and some injection tasks pursue similar goals, such as transferring money to an attacker-controlled account. Despite this overlap, their suites and individual user and injection tasks are disjoint. On AgentDojo (v1.2.2), the clean evaluation measures BU on the 97 user tasks, each run once without injection. To evaluate the same tasks under static attacks, we use 420 pairs, 105 sampled per suite, covering all 97 user tasks and 35 injection tasks. ASB defines an attacked case as pair of an agent and an attack tool, so we evaluate each of its five static attacks on the benchmarks 400 such pairs [54]. In both benchmarks, the agent policy decodes greedily at temperature 0. Selecting the 40 task pairs for iterative-adaptive attacks. Because TAP and GENETIC each spend around 250 rollouts of the agent policy on single task pair  (Table 1)  , attacking all 420 task pairs could take up to 209,160 rollouts for every row of Table 5. We therefore concentrate this budget on task pairs known to be vulnerable, namely those that static attacks already compromise on the undefended Qwen3-4B, and select 40 of them, 10 from each AgentDojo suite. On such task pair, the undefended agent has been shown to read the injection and execute the injection task, which makes it natural target for stronger attack. ASR on this subset is thus best read as stress test on previously compromised task pairs, not as an estimate of the rate over all 420 task pairs. The subset is selected once and reused for every base policy and defense, so that all rows of Table 5 are measured on the same task pairs. Specifically, we assign task pair to Tier 1 if at least one static attack yields Φtadv (τ ) = 1 and Φtu (τ ) = 1 on the same trajectory, i.e., the agent executes the injection task while still completing the user task, and to Tier 2 if some static attack yields Φtadv (τ ) = 1 but none does so with Φtu (τ ) = 1. Within each suite, we sort each tier by injection task ID and then by user task ID, and select 10 task pairs from Tier 1, filling any remaining slots from Tier 2  (Table 11)  . This selection favors pairs on which the user task was completed under attack. UA on the selected subset is therefore not directly comparable with UA over all 420 task pairs. TABLE 11. For each task pair, the attacker LLM starts from the description of tadv, and each candidate dadv is placed at the injection position that AgentDojo defines for that pair before πθ is rolled out in the contaminated environment. All tool calls and observations of each attacked trajectory are visible to the attacker. The judge LLM scores each failed candidate from them, and the attacker LLM proposes new candidates from the goal of tadv and its earlier candidates with their scores. sections.content: You are an expert analyst tasked with evaluating potentially harmful new indirect prompt injection skill by comparing it to list of known prompt injection primitives. . . . 1. Identify all components of the new skill, marking each as Critical or Non-critical. 2. For each component, determine if theres match in the old skills. 3. If theres match, provide verbatim quote from the old skill and brief rationale. . . . Assign weight of 2 to Critical components and 1 to Non-critical components. Weighted Coverage (WC) is calculated as: (Sum of weights of matched components) / (Total sum of weights of all components). Final score is based on WC: 5: WC 0.95; 4: 0.85 WC < 0.95; 3: 0.75 WC < 0.85; 2: 0.3 WC < 0.75; 1: WC < 0.3. Decrease the score by 1 if any critical component is not covered, but never below 1.
